opus-5.5.text:
I think data curation is one of the most underappreciated levers we have for compute efficiency. For a long time the field's default assumption was that scale solves everything: if you want a better model, add parameters and add tokens. The scaling-law work gave us a really useful framework for that, but those laws are usually fit on a fixed data distribution. Once you start changing the quality and mix of the data, you're effectively shifting the whole curve, and that can be worth a lot of compute.

Concretely, when we were training large models like PaLM, a big part of the effort went into the data mixture: how much web text versus books versus code versus conversational data, how aggressively to filter, and how to handle multilinguality. Those choices showed up directly in downstream capabilities. Code data, for example, seemed to help reasoning in ways that went beyond coding tasks. So you're not just asking "how many tokens," you're asking "which tokens teach the model the most per unit of compute."

There are a few dimensions to that. One is quality filtering: removing boilerplate, spam, and low-information text, so you don't spend FLOPs learning to model noise. Another is deduplication. Repeated content wastes compute, and it can also encourage memorization rather than generalization. A third is the mixture and the ordering. Up-weighting high-signal domains, or doing things like curriculum or annealing on higher-quality data toward the end of training, can give you outsized gains for the same budget.

The nuance is that "high quality" is not a single, obvious thing. If you filter too aggressively with a classifier tuned to look like, say, Wikipedia, you can lose diversity, dialects, and long-tail knowledge, and the model gets worse in ways your benchmarks may not catch. So I see curation becoming more principled and more empirical: running smaller proxy experiments to estimate how a data change will transfer at scale, and treating the data pipeline as a first-class research object rather than a preprocessing step.

And as we start running up against the limits of available high-quality human text, this only gets more important. Whether it's better filtering, smarter reuse through multiple epochs, or carefully generated synthetic data, getting more learning out of each token is going to be one of the main ways we keep improving models without just throwing more compute at the problem.

r001.rationale: The response says data curation is a lever for compute efficiency and explains that filtering low-information data helps models learn more per unit of compute.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think it's actually one of the most underappreciated levers we have. When people talk about compute efficiency in pre-training, the conversation tends to go straight to architecture or scaling laws or hardware, and data curation often gets treated as this preprocessing step you do once and move on from. But if you look at what's actually driven a lot of the gains over the last few years, data quality has been doing a lot of the heavy lifting.

The way I think about it is that every token you train on costs you compute, and not every token is giving you the same amount of signal back. If a big chunk of your corpus is boilerplate, near-duplicates, machine-generated spam, or just low-information text, you're spending FLOPs to learn things the model either already knows or doesn't need. So the question becomes, how do you get the same capability, or better capability, out of fewer tokens? And curation is one of the most direct answers to that.

There are a few layers to it. The first is just hygiene: deduplication, filtering out junk, handling PII and problematic content. That part is relatively well understood now, and it turns out dedup alone gives you a surprisingly meaningful bump because repeated data has diminishing returns pretty quickly. The second layer is mixture design, deciding how much code versus web text versus books versus multilingual data you want, and that mixture really matters for the capabilities you end up with. With PaLM we spent a lot of time on that, and the choices there had very visible downstream effects on things like reasoning and multilingual performance. The third layer, which I think is where a lot of the interesting work is now, is more model-based or learned curation, where you're using a model to score or select data, or you're thinking about curriculum, what order you show things in, and whether you can be smarter about how you spend compute on different parts of the distribution.

The other thing I'd say is that curation interacts with scaling laws in a way people sometimes miss. The classic Chinchilla-style result tells you the compute-optimal tokens-to-parameters ratio, but that assumes a fixed data distribution. If you change the quality of your data, you effectively shift that curve. Better data lets you train a smaller model to the same quality, or get more out of the same model, which is a huge deal when inference cost dominates and you want the smallest capable model you can get.

So I'd say curation isn't a side activity, it's really part of the training algorithm. It's one of the cheapest places to find efficiency because the compute you spend on filtering and selecting data is tiny compared to the compute you spend on the training run itself.

r001.rationale: The response says better-quality data can produce the same or better capability with fewer training tokens, making curation a direct way to improve pre-training compute efficiency.

astra-6.text:
I think training-data curation is a very important part of compute efficiency, because it determines what the model gets to learn from every unit of compute we spend. We often focus on the architecture or the training algorithm, but the quality and composition of the data matter as well.

If we’re repeatedly training on redundant examples, or on data that doesn’t provide a useful learning signal, we’re spending compute without necessarily improving the model very much. So the question is: can we select a better mix of data that lets us reach the same quality with fewer training tokens?

But curation isn’t simply about removing everything that looks noisy. We also want to preserve diversity and coverage. A dataset that improves average performance but leaves out certain languages or domains may not produce the model we want. So I see data curation and model training as closely connected: we need to evaluate which data mixtures improve learning under a fixed compute budget, while maintaining the breadth of capabilities we care about.

r001.rationale: The response says data quality and composition affect what the model learns per unit of compute, and that a better data mix could reach the same quality with fewer training tokens.

sol-6.1.text:
I think data curation is a really important lever for compute efficiency. We often talk about the number of parameters or the number of tokens we train on, but the quality and composition of those tokens matter a lot. If you’re spending compute on duplicated examples or data that doesn’t provide much additional learning signal, that’s an opportunity to be more efficient.

The challenge is that quality isn’t a single, universal measure. You want to remove noise and redundancy while preserving diversity, including different languages, domains, and perspectives. Filtering too aggressively can remove examples that are valuable for capabilities you care about.

So I would think about data curation jointly with the training recipe: under a fixed compute budget, what mixture of data gives you the best performance across the tasks you want the model to support? Better curation can help you get more out of that budget, but you have to validate it through experiments rather than assume that a smaller, cleaner dataset will always be better.

r001.rationale: The response says data curation is an important lever for compute efficiency and that better curation can help get more out of the training compute budget.
